summary: All waves are integrated on branch perf-trial-20260906-030748 (hub). main is untouched. 52/52 tests pass (28 at baseline), and every optimization is guarded by a regression or tradeoff-pinning test.

The library's biggest cost was the dependency-free EPUB zip writer: a pure-JS CRC32 loop (Node ships a native one — 70× faster), deflate level 9 applied to JPEG scans that compress 0% at any level, and a final whole-archive buffer copy. Fixing all three took EPUB assembly of a 13 MB magazine from ~189 ms to ~7 ms and cut peak memory 26%, with output marginally smaller than baseline.

The interface's biggest cost was serial round trips: every REST call paid a fresh TLS handshake (no keep-alive), audiobook parts downloaded one at a time, and a magazine's pages/assets were fetched one at a time — a 300-page magazine spent minutes waiting on the network. Measured against a local latency-injecting TLS server: connection reuse halved a 30-request loopback run (each saved handshake is worth 50–150 ms against the real OverDrive hosts), and bounded 4-way concurrency turned 120 × 25 ms requests from 3.2 s into 0.83 s (3.84×).
One candidate was measured and rejected: lazy-loading CLI commands (≤9 ms ceiling, invisible next to process spawn). It stays recorded so nobody re-litigates it.

waves.name: Native CRC32 in the EPUB zip writer
waves.change: Replaced the 256-entry-table pure-JS CRC32 loop in src/epub.mjs with Node's native zlib.crc32.
tradeoffs: engines floor moved from >=20 to >=20.15 (zlib.crc32 availability) — done in package.json
CRC outputs verified byte-identical by the bench

waves.name: Store already-compressed media instead of deflating
waves.change: zip() ran deflate level 9 over every entry. JPEG/PNG/GIF/webp/avif/MP3/MP4/m4a/PDF payloads compress 0% (measured ratio 1.000 at levels 6 and 9) — they are now STORED, like the mimetype entry always was.
tradeoffs: A mislabeled media file (a .jpg that is really uncompressed data) would now be carried raw — in practice scan assets are real JPEGs, and the whole EPUB came out ~0.2% SMALLER than baseline (no deflate overhead on incompressible bytes)
EPUB readers accept stored entries (spec-compliant); unzip -t clean, and now asserted in test/epub-integrity.test.mjs

waves.name: Deflate level 9 → 6 for compressible entries
waves.change: Text/XHTML entries deflate at level 6: 2× faster for ratio 0.088 → 0.090.
tradeoffs: Text entries grow ~2%; whole-EPUB impact well under 1% because image scans dominate the bytes
One-line revert if the owner prefers level 9

waves.name: Single-allocation zip assembly (peak RAM)
waves.change: zip() built a chunk list then Buffer.concat'd the entire EPUB a second time. It now writes into one preallocated buffer (deflate first to learn sizes, then fill).
tradeoffs: Compressed entries still exist transiently (synchronous deflate cannot target an existing buffer). A streaming zip-to-file would cut peak further but changes the public API — left for the owner to want
During the rewrite an allocUnsafe EOCD zero-fill bug was introduced and caught by unzip -t; a test now asserts those fields

waves.name: Faster __bif_cfc1 page-blob decode
waves.change: read.mjs decoded every read-host page with a regex replace (per-match overhead at MB scale). Replaced with a hand-rolled code-unit quad-swap loop that is exactly equivalent — including the subtle rule that groups containing line terminators pass through and realign scanning.
tradeoffs: Equivalence property-tested against the original regex: deterministic hostile-input sweep + hand-computed edges (4n±k lengths, terminators) in test/read.test.mjs

waves.name: Parallel integrity-manifest hashing
waves.change: writeManifest() hashed files one stream at a time; now ~8 files in flight with 1 MiB reads, order preserved.
tradeoffs: Warm-cache gain is modest because SHA-256 runs at hardware speed on M4 and the cache absorbs I/O; the win grows on cold caches/slower disks and larger archives
Output is byte-identical to the sequential implementation — pinned in test/manifest-ref.test.mjs against a vendored copy of the old algorithm

waves.name: Keep-alive HTTP connection pooling
waves.change: REST calls used Node's default global agent (keepAlive off): every Thunder/stargazer/cover/page request paid a fresh TLS handshake. One pooled agent per TLS mode now: keepAlive, maxSockets 8, maxFreeSockets 4, 30 s keep-alive, noDelay, agent-level timeout backstop — with the per-request timeout/destroy handlers untouched so the historic wedge failure stays closed.
tradeoffs: Loopback understates the win: each avoided handshake is worth ~50–150 ms against the real OverDrive hosts
Up to 4 idle sockets per host linger ≤30 s; CLI exit closes them
Pinned by tests: reuse count, hung-socket timeout, 12-over-8 drain (test/http.test.mjs)

waves.name: Concurrent audiobook part downloads
waves.change: Spine parts download 3 at a time (mapLimit) instead of strictly sequentially. Skip/resume logic, per-part logs, fail-fast, and spine order preserved.
tradeoffs: 3 simultaneous CDN connections per title — deliberately low (the browser uses 6+)
Part-level failure still aborts the loan; resume unchanged

waves.name: Concurrent page + asset fetching (ebooks/magazines)
waves.change: Pages fetch+decode 4 at a time, then assets 4 at a time (both were serial — a 300-page magazine was 300 round trips). pageEntries stay in spine order for EPUB assembly; non-200 assets still log-and-skip; first page error rejects the loan.
tradeoffs: In-flight page/asset bodies raise steady-state RAM by the concurrency factor (bounded, a few MB)
Page logs now report decoded (completed) pages so numbers stay truthful under interleaving
Also removed: dead width variable in archive-read step 4

waves.name: CLI lazy command loading
waves.change: Considered splitting bin/libby.mjs imports per command. Measured first: the full import graph costs ~9 ms over the bare Node floor (36.4 vs 27.3 ms for libby help).
tradeoffs: Rejected: ≤9 ms upside is invisible next to process spawn cost; dynamic imports would move load errors from startup to command time. Recorded so nobody re-litigates it.

waves.name: Regression + tradeoff-pinning test wave
waves.change: Test suite grew 28 → 52. New: pooled-HTTP properties (socket reuse counted server-side, hung-socket timeout, 12-over-8 drain), downloadPart over pooled connections (redirect, exact bytes + sha256, truncated-body rejection with .part cleanup), EPUB spec validity via unzip -t, store/deflate method pins, stored-entry CRC pin, size-tradeoff pins (text still compresses <40%, stored media adds ≤1 KB overhead), manifest byte-identity vs the vendored sequential reference, and a proper fail-fast pin for mapLimit (the original lane test passed only by timing accident — the bug it masked was real and is now fixed).
tradeoffs: The EPUB size pins encode this campaign's CPU-vs-storage choices: if a future change re-inflates stored media or stops compressing text, the suite fails with the tradeoff in the message

waves.name: Streaming EPUB writer (peak RAM)
waves.change: New writeZip/writeEpub stream the archive to disk entry-by-entry (atomic .part + rename) instead of materializing the whole EPUB in memory — peak moves from O(archive) to O(largest entry). zip()/buildEpub stay with byte-identical output (pinned by test); archiveReadable now writes via writeEpub; entriesFor/writeZip/writeEpub are exported from the library index.

metrics.name: peak RSS producing 12.7 MB EPUB (writeZip vs zip)
same, vs the 108 MB the campaign started from
wall time for that EPUB (zip → writeZip)

tradeoffs: Streaming is ~1.5× slower in wall time than one big memcpy — trivial in absolute terms (~15 ms) — and the RAM saving scales with archive size
Archive size is known only after the write; the write path is async

Follow-up identified, not in scope: page/asset body arrays still hold decoded content in RAM while assembling — a lazy from-disk loader (zipChunks already accepts async sources) would cut the remaining resident set

waves.name: Openbook decode (descramble + literal parser)
waves.change: decodeOpenbook ran parseFloat per character (key shifts are per-position constants — precomputed once) and scanned string literals character-by-character (now copies whole runs between escapes/quotes with identical escape semantics). Runs once per archived loan, on a player page that can exceed 2 MB.
tradeoffs: Outputs verified identical by the bench (JSON deep-equal) and the full test suite

First rewrite used sticky regexes (match-at-index only), which swallowed closing quotes — the existing single-quoted-literal test caught it immediately; fixed to global/next-occurrence semantics. Proof the regression net pays.

waves.name: Auth/checkout path examination
waves.change: Examined auth.mjs/sentry.mjs/checkout.mjs for wins. The auth handshake (mint chip → link card → sync code → clone → remint) is protocol-ordered and cached across runs by the session file; sentry.mjs already keeps one pooled agent; search/checkout are 1–2 calls.
tradeoffs: Rejected: nothing to parallelize without violating the chip protocol's ordering; per-invocation cost is already amortized by the session cache. Recorded so the surface isn't re-swept without new information.

waves.name: End-to-end archive tests against a simulated OverDrive
waves.change: New e2e suite drives the REAL orchestrators (archiveAudiobook / archiveReadable) through loan open → session handshake → openbook decode → downloads → EPUB/sidecars → integrity manifest against three local TLS hosts serving the genuine wire formats (scrambled window.eData player pages, __bif_cfc1 page bodies, CDN-style part redirects). Only the credential boundary (authenticate/sentry) is stubbed. Building it flushed out two real bugs: CookieJar and jsonRequest silently mis-connected when a host carried an explicit port (both now parse host:port), and it caught the W13 sticky-regex quote bug the day it was written. Thunder got a LIBBY_THUNDER_HOST test seam.
tradeoffs: One-line test seam in metadata.mjs (env-overridable Thunder host) — production default unchanged
Tests skip gracefully when openssl is unavailable

waves.name: Disk-backed EPUB payloads (assembly RAM)
waves.change: archiveReadable retained every decoded page body and asset buffer while assembling the EPUB — the whole book resident, and duplicated, even though the pages/assets were already written to disk. Entry payloads can now be thunks (() => read-from-disk) resolved once at encode time; the orchestrator passes lazy readers instead of buffers, so assembly no longer holds the book in RAM.

metrics.name: peak RSS producing 12.7 MB EPUB (buffer vs disk-backed entries)

tradeoffs: Resident payload memory now scales with the largest entry, not the book; the remaining 55 MB is mostly the Node floor (~48 MB)
A payload file vanishing between write and read fails the archive loudly mid-stream (ENOENT, .part cleaned) — pinned by test; wall time unchanged (≈206 ms both paths in the bench harness)
Methodology: fresh process per impl, RSS sampled at entry boundaries — one-shot RSS masks the win on macOS (freed pages are never returned)

waves.name: Hash-once integrity pass
waves.change: downloadPart already computes each part’s sha256 while streaming, and archive.mjs was throwing it away — so writeManifest re-read the entire book to hash what had just been hashed. Part digests are now carried into writeManifest(dir, { known }), which trusts exact digests for matching files and only re-reads content nobody hashed (sidecars, cover, README).

metrics.name: integrity pass, 50 MB archive, digests known

tradeoffs: Known digests are trusted, not re-verified (re-verifying would defeat the purpose); a streaming writer bug would surface as a bad manifest — the e2e suite validates every manifest line against file contents to police exactly this
Skipped (already-present) parts have no digest and are re-hashed as before — correct, since their bytes were not observed this run
Warm-cache M4 numbers; on cold caches the win is a full re-read of the book avoided

waves.name: Compact raw sidecars (storage)
waves.change: Considered minifying the raw machine sidecars (openbook.json, thunder.json, passport.json, loan.json) instead of pretty-printing them. Measured on realistically-shaped records: the big one barely benefits.

metrics.name: openbook.json at magazine scale (~1.9 MB, bulk = one description string)
thunder.json (rich catalog record, 45% smaller but only KBs)

tradeoffs: Rejected: ~1% on the only large sidecar (its bulk is a whitespace-free payload string; indent only costs on structure) and KBs elsewhere — tens of KB per archive, not worth losing human-readable provenance records
Measurement kept: perf/storage-sidecars.mjs; helper reverted before merge

waves.name: Streamed EPUB digest (no re-read at manifest time)
waves.change: writeZip hashes every byte as it streams and returns { bytes, sha256 }; archiveReadable feeds that digest into writeManifest({ known }) keyed by the EPUB basename. The largest file in a magazine archive is no longer re-read and re-hashed by the integrity pass.
tradeoffs: Same trusted-digest contract as W17 — the magazine e2e re-hashes every manifest line against file contents on the real path, which is the acceptance
Digest correctness pinned: writeZip sha256 must equal a fresh re-hash of the written file

waves.name: Catalog round trips overlap downloads
waves.change: The thunder metadata fetch + cover download ran strictly before the download loops in both orchestrators; they are now started before and awaited where first needed — ~2 serial round trips (~200–400 ms against OverDrive) come off every archived loan.
tradeoffs: Only observable change: catalog log lines can interleave with download logs (message content unchanged)
Failure semantics preserved exactly: thunder null-tolerant, cover keeps its try/catch + log; both promises always awaited (no unhandled-rejection window)

waves.name: Cross-loan parallel archiving (archive --all)
waves.change: Considered archiving 2 loans at a time instead of strictly sequentially. Rejected without implementation: OverDrive rate-limits aggressively (the CLI already special-cases the whoa response and exits), multi-loan parallelism multiplies request bursts per card, and the risk cannot be validated offline — the simulated hosts cannot reproduce server-side throttling.
tradeoffs: The safe wins (per-loan concurrency W8/W9, pooling W7, overlap W20) capture most of the wall-clock upside without touching card-level request rates
If the owner ever wants it: make the loan-level concurrency an opt-in flag, default 1, and validate against a real shelf

adoption: Everything from all waves lives on branch perf-trial-20260906-103453 (branched from the wave-3 tip, which holds waves W1–W17). Each wave is an independent commit; main is untouched.
To adopt everything: git merge perf-trial-20260906-103453 from main (fast-forward). package.json engines is >=20.15 (zlib.crc32).

Behavioral deltas: EPUB bytes differ from baseline by design (stored media, level-6 text) but stay spec-valid and ~0.2% smaller; the EPUB write path is async (writeEpub); raw sidecar write order shifted with W20 (thunder.json lands when its fetch resolves); catalog logs may interleave with download logs; everything else is byte-identical (manifests, decoded content).

Reproducible: node --test (65), node --expose-gc perf/bench.mjs, node perf/net-sim.mjs src current, node --expose-gc perf/zip-stream-one.mjs zip|writeZip, node --expose-gc perf/zip-thunk-one.mjs prepare. Lane notes: perf-notes-cpu.md / perf-notes-net.md / perf-notes-ram.md / perf-notes-w16.md / perf-notes-orch.md.
